target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, and safety
objection: AI’s benefits come with serious costs that often fall on ordinary people, so the net effect is not automatically positive.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves economic well-being by automating routine tasks
objection: Automation is not neutral: it can reduce workers’ and small businesses’ income and bargaining power, concentrating gains in large firms while displaced people absorb retraining and unemployment costs.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves health outcomes
objection: Health benefits are not guaranteed because many AI systems are opaque and trained on biased or incomplete data, which can create unequal performance and worsen disparities.

target: AG1’s claim that AI increases accessibility for marginalized groups
objection: Accessibility tools may require sensitive personal data such as voice, images, or location, so they can be tied to intrusive privacy and surveillance tradeoffs.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves workplace safety
objection: AI safety systems can fail silently, misclassify situations, or shift responsibility away from companies and onto users, creating new risks instead of reducing them.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps students and professionals by supporting learning and work
objection: Using AI for drafting, problem-solving, and fact-checking can reduce people’s motivation and ability to reason independently, eroding critical thinking skills.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be fairly and beneficially used if managed responsibly
objection: AI systems can repeat and amplify historical racism because they learn from biased data, worsening outcomes for racial minorities in hiring, policing-adjacent tools, lending, education, and recommendations.

target: AG1’s proposal that AI harms can be controlled through policy, privacy-by-design, oversight, safety engineering, education design, and bias auditing
objection: Those safeguards are hard to enforce at scale because companies profit from data extraction, automation, and rapid rollout, so responsible use is often structurally unlikely in real deployments.

target: AG1’s assumption that human oversight can reliably catch AI errors
objection: Human supervision is not a dependable fix because it requires time, staffing, and training that many organizations lack, and it can become a rubber stamp that merely shifts blame after failures.

target: AG1’s claim that education design and AI literacy can preserve critical thinking
objection: Even with better assignments, students and adults still have incentives to use AI to generate answers quickly, so critical thinking erosion remains difficult to prevent without intrusive monitoring.

target: AG1’s claim that bias can be reduced through auditing, better datasets, fairness constraints, and documentation
objection: Those measures may reduce some harms but cannot eliminate bias rooted in unequal systems, and affected groups often lack meaningful recourse when models cause harm.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks can be solved through privacy-by-design and user consent
objection: Assistive and other practical AI tools often require sensitive data pipelines, and in many real settings privacy-by-design is not adopted while consent is only nominal because users have few alternatives.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because governance can align incentives and make safeguards enforceable
objection: The need for constant guardrails itself shows the technology’s deployment is structurally risky, and society cannot rely on incentives being realigned well enough to make AI broadly beneficial.

target: AG1’s claim that broader net benefit is enough to call AI good for society
objection: Governance and audits cannot keep up with fast-changing, opaque AI systems, and liability often fails to assign clear responsibility when harms arise from complex pipelines.

target: AG1’s claim that enforceable rules can prevent harmful AI deployment
objection: Regulatory capture and global competition pressure oversight toward minimal compliance, so companies can still push harmful rollouts faster than regulators can respond.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be broadly beneficial despite risks
objection: AI creates new scalable harms such as misinformation, manipulation, deepfakes, fraud, and identity abuse that can damage public discourse and financial security even when individual systems appear safe.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous monitoring can solve moving-target AI risks
objection: Continuous monitoring expands surveillance and privacy harms because it requires collecting detailed user, device, or behavioral data, which especially burdens racial minorities and low-income groups.

target: AG1’s claim that provenance and detection tools can counter synthetic misinformation
objection: Detection and watermarking face a cat-and-mouse problem: attackers can quickly adapt generation methods and evade markers, so defenders cannot reliably neutralize the scale of abuse.

target: AG1’s claim that AI-based fraud and identity protections reduce harm
objection: Fraud detection and authentication often depend on broader data sharing and centralized aggregation, which increases the same privacy risks the defense is supposed to solve.

target: AG1’s claim that governance and safeguards can be applied broadly enough to make AI good for society
objection: The strongest safeguards are expensive and operationally complex, so they are more available to large firms and well-resourced institutions, while smaller businesses and individuals remain more exposed.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring can avoid surveillance harms
objection: Even privacy-preserving analytics still require enough data to detect deepfakes, fraud, or malicious behavior, which pushes systems toward surveillance-by-architecture and centralized control.

target: AG1’s claim that cryptographic provenance and signing can reliably solve misinformation problems
objection: Provenance only works if major platforms adopt and honor verification, and it can become a gatekeeping system that disadvantages unverified content and potentially marginalized groups.

target: AG1’s claim that layered defenses can keep pace with AI abuse
objection: Attackers can generate persuasive variants cheaply and continuously, so defenses may reduce harm at the margins but do not eliminate the underlying scalability asymmetry.

target: AG1’s conclusion that AI is good for society overall if paired with heavy governance
objection: If AI needs constant, sophisticated governance, centralized monitoring, and ecosystem-wide technical compliance to avoid foreseeable harm, then its broad societal deployment is not reliably net positive.
